Today we are announcing Harvey LAB-AA v1.1 in collaboration with Harvey. This updates our scoring methodology for the Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) to add a hallucination check and require correct responses to not include material misstatements. LAB-AA v1.1's new headline metric, Hallucination-Gated All-Pass Rate, only credits a task when the deliverables satisfy every rubric criterion and contain no material hallucinations.

We define a material hallucination as one that would mislead a reader on a substantive point, such as a wrong contractually required date, while a minor hallucination is a real error that is unlikely to meaningfully affect the legal interpretation of a deliverable. Minor hallucinations are reported separately and do not affect the headline score.

Grok 4.7 (xhigh) leads at 9.4% Hallucination-Gated All-Pass Rate, and >60% of otherwise passing results across the models tested at launch contain a material hallucination.

This is the first step in enhancing the methodology for Harvey LAB-AA. In future updates, we’re working with Harvey to better account for the full set of factors lawyers value, including usability features like style and tone.

Key takeaways:

➤ Top of the leaderboard: Grok 4.7 (xhigh) from @SpaceXAI leads at 9.4% Hallucination-Gated All-Pass Rate, narrowly ahead of Muse Spark 1.3 (max) from @AIatMeta at 8.9% and GPT-6 Astra (max) from @OpenAI at 8.6%

➤ Hallucinations reshape the leaderboard: without the hallucination gate, Muse Spark 1.3 (max) would lead clearly with a 26.7% all-pass rate, but two thirds of those passes contain one or more material hallucinations, resulting in a Hallucination-Gated All-Pass Rate of 8.9%. GPT-6 Astra (max) retains almost all of its passes after the hallucination gate (8.9% to 8.6%) and moves from joint 10th to 3rd

➤ Top-scoring models aren’t the most expensive: Grok 4.7 (xhigh) takes the top spot on the leaderboard at a cost of ~$9.50 per task, under half the cost of Claude Fable 5.1 (max with fallback) at ~$21.70, the most expensive model. reposted.text:
David Sacks: The Economy Is Stronger Than You Think

“There's been a tremendous amount of economic data in just the last week or two showing that the economy is much stronger than people are giving it credit for.

So first of all, Q2 GDP was revised up to 2.2% from 1.5%, so that's basically a 50% increase. Economists had expected no revision. Q1 was also revised up to 2.5% from 2.1%. And if you look at the Q3 growth, it's tracking well above that. The Atlanta Fed GDPNow is showing around 3.7% as of late last week.

And then there was also some good news on inflation, we saw that core PCE just came in at 3.0% versus 3.3% expected. So inflation is still a bit too high, but actually it is cooling and beating expectations.

And then finally, you look at manufacturing. We're seeing a huge wave of re-industrialization in this country. A couple of the measures are the Chicago PMI and then ISM Manufacturing. They both are well into expansion territory and beating forecasts.

Just one last point, let's talk about poverty for a second, because I want to address the idea that this is just a K-shaped recovery.

So if you look at US household income, it's now at record high. The median household income is almost $90,000, and after-tax household income is growing again in the second Trump term, it's averaged 3.1% a year. In Trump 47, it was 3.9%, in Trump 45, and it was -1.2% in Biden's term as a four-year average. So we're seeing that after-tax household incomes have risen by 3.1%, and the poverty rate in the US has fallen to its lowest level in history, 10.2%.

So the poverty rate, the child poverty rate, these are all at historic lows. The average household's real income after inflation, after taxes, is increasing for the first time in years.

And you've got this SI boom that the Wall Street Journal said is bigger than the railroads, the canals, and the electric grid combined, and all these things are basically fueling strong growth in the economy.

And again, I would just dispute the K-shaped narrative because the poor are benefiting and the average household are benefiting as well.”

posts.name: Ray Dalio
posts.text:
Over long periods of time, debts tend to rise faster than incomes, creating the long-term debt cycle.

Even as people become more indebted, lenders freely extend credit because during economic booms, incomes rise, asset values soar, and the stock market thrives. People borrow more to buy financial assets, pushing prices higher and creating a bubble.

So long as incomes keep rising, the debt burden stays manageable. But this cannot continue forever. Over decades, debt burdens slowly accumulate until debt repayments grow faster than incomes. This forces people to cut back on spending, causing incomes to fall and borrowing to dry up—eventually reversing the entire cycle.
#RayDalio #Economy #LongTermDebtCycle #Finance

We are seeing a total failure of MMT around the globe.

QE and deficit spending (after 2008 and during COVID) was basically an attempt at Modern Monetary Theory (MMT).  In a nutshell, MMT says that we can print and deficit spend at will without any fiscal or economic complications.

So, central banks held interest rates at zero, forcing markets to accept absurdly low rates.  At the same time, these central banks printed massive amounts of money and absorbed a lot of this new debt themselves.

MMTers said we could do this with no inflation.  Clearly they were wrong.  Friedman taught us exactly what would happen, and it did.  Inflation took off.  The result, central banks were forced to raise rates and stop expanding their balance sheets.

So far, governments have resisted fiscal sanity and are still running massive deficits even though central banks stopped funding them.  

The result?  In the past 3 months, 10-year bond yields are up 50 bps in the UK, 90 bps in France, 72 bps in the US, and more than 40 bps in Germany.

Governments were already too big in 2008, but this crazy experiment over the past 18 years has pushed things toward a breaking point.

France proposes to freeze government pay and pensions, and raise some taxes and we should expect more movement toward austerity in other countries soon.

MMT is basically Keynesianism on steroids.  It didn’t work.  The fix is a revival of Austrian, supply-side economics.  Smaller governments, lower tax rates, tighter money, and less regulation.  Some will say this is a pipe dream.  But it is the only way out.

BREAKING: OpenAI’s solution to Navier–Stokes does not match its Lean verification.

The most important article to read today is not one of OpenAI’s 700 AI-generated math papers.

It is this other paper, making a deep and worrying point:

A Lean-verified proof does not automatically validate the proof written in natural language, nor does it mean that the formal statement captures the intended theorem.

During translation, an AI can change an assumption, weaken a statement, or replace the argument entirely.

It can hallucinate another theorem.

Lean correctly verifies the result.
But the proved result may no longer be what the paper claims.

This is a general problem. Things get spicy when the authors examine OpenAI’s proposed Navier–Stokes solution.

They identify at least two mismatches between the written intermediate results and their Lean counterparts:

One estimate claims that four additional input derivatives suffice. The Lean version requires five: a weaker result.

A pressure-flux estimate is obtained through a different bound, and proved through a different argument.

It is not clear whether these mismatches invalidate the entire proof.

But they raise an important issue.

OpenAI is flooding us with claimed revolutionary breakthroughs. Yet nobody knows whether the proofs are correct or whether they prove what they claim to be proving.

Epistemia at scale.

reposted.text:
What Today’s Jobless Claims Really Reveal

The October 8 unemployment claims report exposes a labor market where layoffs remain subdued but hiring is increasingly weak. The headline looks reassuring, but the underlying figures tell a more complicated story.

Initial claims fell 2,000 to 197,000, but the previous week was revised upward from 197,000 to 199,000. Today’s reading is identical to last week’s original estimate.

The 4 week average declined to 198,000, partly because an older 207,000 reading rolled out.

What The Seasonal Adjustments Reveal

Actual initial claims increased 11,994 to 170,333, a 7.6% increase.

The seasonal model anticipated 13,725 additional claims. Because filings rose by 1,731 fewer than expected, the adjusted headline registered a decline.

This does not establish seasonal overcorrection. It means the improvement was relative to seasonal expectations rather than an actual decline in applications.

Continuing claims present the more concerning signal.

Adjusted claims increased 17,000 to 1.716 million. Actual claims increased 7,579 when the seasonal model anticipated a decline of 6,798.

That leaves continuing claims 14,377 above the expected seasonal path.

Instead of the normal seasonal improvement, more people continued claiming benefits.

However, the 4 week average still declined to 1.711 million, partly because an older 1.765 million reading rolled out.

The State Data Reveal Something Deeper

California added 4,578 initial claims, Illinois 1,154 and New York 985.

Together, these states accounted for 56% of the national increase in actual filings.

California, Washington and Oregon collectively recorded 14,931 additional continuing claims, nearly twice the national increase of 7,579.

Across the remaining jurisdictions, continuing claims actually declined by 7,352.

This suggests concentrated regional pressure rather than established nationwide deterioration.

Nevertheless, 35 of 53 reporting jurisdictions recorded increasing initial claims, although some increase was seasonally expected.

Another overlooked development involves worksharing benefits.

Claims associated with reduced working hours increased 7.1% to 13,222. They remain below last year’s levels, but businesses can reduce hours and overtime before eliminating positions.

State additional benefit claims also increased approximately 32% from a year earlier, although volumes remain small and program rules vary.

Meanwhile, continuing claims have declined more slowly than initial claims over the past year. That warrants monitoring for longer unemployment spells, although it does not independently establish slower reemployment.

The Bigger Economic Warning

Initial claims remain 15.5% below their year earlier level, while continuing claims are roughly 11% lower.

Those improvements are meaningful. Widespread layoffs have not materialized in this report.

But low layoffs do not automatically establish healthy labor demand.

Hiring remains subdued, quits are depressed and employment growth is weak.

Companies can retain existing employees while reducing recruitment, overtime and working hours.

That creates an economy where unemployment appears contained even as opportunities for displaced workers deteriorate.

This is why the unexpected increase in continuing claims deserves attention.

Businesses are already confronting elevated borrowing costs, refinancing pressure, deteriorating credit conditions and compressed operating margins.

If employers begin reducing payrolls, displaced workers could encounter a labor market with insufficient hiring capacity to absorb them.

Unemployment could then accelerate, weakening consumption, business revenues and ultimately employment further.

That is how apparent stability can transition into a self reinforcing economic contraction.

The greatest risk is not how many people are losing jobs today. The economy may have lost much of its ability to absorb unemployment before widespread layoffs begin.

AI has become the umbrella term for nearly everything happening in tech today. That term caught on first. But when you consider what companies like Tesla and SpaceX are ultimately trying to achieve, I think "super intelligence" (SI) is a more accurate description of their ambitions.

At first I thought SI was a silly term to use over AI, but after thinking about it, Tesla and SpaceX are trying to create a real super intelligence, and less so an "artificial intelligence." Think about how we describe someone who's exceptionally smart. We say they're "super intelligent." Nobody says they're "artificially intelligent."

SI would have been a better term from the beginning. A lot of people will probably still call it AI, but Optimus is not going to be artificially intelligent, it's going to have super intelligence. It'll take some getting used to lol

And it's the first time anyone's ever seen anything quite like it. They also created the largest ever communications satellite network, Starlink.

And in North Carolina, I will tell you personally, because I was involved, we had a hurricane, one of the great water hurricanes of all time, delivered more water than at any time that we can remember on record. But you are a very, very special guy. Thank you very much, and congratulations, Elon. Thank you."

I’ve had countless people on this app argue with me that Anthropic has a $65BN ARR.

Here’s a quick lesson on the discrepancy between venture capital power point math and real accounting math.

OPEN AI IS MINUS $20BN AND THEY ARE NOT YET PCOAB AUDITED.

Privately, I made a bet with several people on this app, payable in pushups, that Anthropic would see a $20BN revenue write down. Remember the difference, OpenAI is not PC audited (yet) and Anthropic is, their 2026 numbers won’t be reported until April-ish in 2027.  

The fact that Open AI voluntarily abandoned fake venture math power point accounting for some real accounting means they are getting ahead of it and Sam Altman is an operator.  This is bite one.  A PC audit will drive them down further. Maybe as much as $10BN more.

No, Oracle and NVIDIA coupons are not revenue.  No, they are not arms length transactions. 

Where Anthropic reports $65BN run rate for 2026, I expect it to be $45BN or less. If I’m right, the other guys do 100 pushups. If I’m wrong, I do 100 pushups. 

There’s also something important to learn about companies spending at Anthropic - a lot of this is one time CAPEX.  Reports have come out about how Facebook and Microsoft used Claude to build their product (in essence, vibe coding), but now the competing products are built and the spend is getting pulled. That’s either a one time CAPEX or an R&D expense.  

Don’t get me wrong, Anthropic has built incredible technology, so good that their competition uses it.

No one that relies on Anthropic will direct the same level of spend towards them in the future.  Use Anthropic to build your tech, then pivot to a lower cost open source model to run the technology. 

I know multiple founders that are getting $20k /month in value from Anthropic for $1k/month, subsidized by Anthropic investors. They are racing to build their product before Anthropic hikes prices. 

Do you think they are ever coming back as customers once their product is built and they have to pay $20k / month?  Not a chance. 

So where does this all land?  Anthropic will have a large IPO (not $2TN) and will be the premier frontier AI model.  

The market will have to adjust their pricing on the stock to account for a significant portion of Anthropic’s revenue to be one time spend in lieu of ARR.

Open AI will watch carefully and fix what they can ahead of their own IPO.

Debt providers and long term contract holders of the AI data centers will have to restructure because they can’t afford for either company to fail. 

For me to buy the Anthropic stock directly, I’m going to need to see that 2026 PCAOB audit first. 

Frontier models will be unprofitable for a long-long time.

The only people that turn a profit in this whole thing are the contractors and developers who built the data centers.

posts.text:
$SBUX $CMG merger offers the wrong kind of synergy.  The overlap between the two brands is unlikely to be enough to justify a takeover premium.

The Financial Times
October 9, 2026

Putting the band back together is surely a great feeling, but a dubious corporate strategy. Starbucks chief Brian Niccol has considered a merger with Chipotle, his $41bn rival — and former employer — the FT reported on Thursday. However neat the match might seem from Starbucks’ corner office, it makes little sense for shareholders.

Niccol knows Chipotle very well indeed. He ran the Mexican-themed restaurant chain for six years before decamping in 2024 to the world’s biggest coffee chain, which was then in a state of considerable disarray. Seen from afar, the two do faintly similar things, serving comestibles to customers who are in a hurry. Both have large, sometimes restive workforces.
Moreover, the ways in which they differ might seem from a distance like opportunities. Chipotle’s balance sheet is free of debt; gearing it up a little could provide low-hanging fruit. And while Starbucks has a sprawling global network, Chipotle has yet to venture outside the US, apart from a smattering of international stores. 

But do these companies really belong together? Not really. For one, the overlap is unlikely to be enough to justify a takeover premium. Imagine Niccol could shave 10 per cent off Chipotle’s food, drink and packaging costs and halve its general overheads. That would save $770mn a year, Lex reckons using Royal Bank of Canada forecasts, giving an after-tax return on investment of just 6 per cent. Anything below 10 per cent should make investors nervous.

More importantly, Niccol hasn’t finished fixing up his present employer, making this a poor time to take on his old one. Starbucks shares have gone sideways since the day his appointment was announced. Profitability isn’t yet where it used to be. Same-store sales growth of 8 per cent in the latest quarter suggests the company has turned a corner, but recent numbers are still flattered by the previous year’s decline.

Chipotle has fared much worse, as has most of the US restaurant sector. But for Niccol to argue he can do a better job than its current leadership might be somewhat problematic, since Chipotle chief Scott Boatwright was his direct report for six years. Conversely, keeping the brand separate and its leaders in place — the Starbucks boss spent more than a decade at multi-brand restaurant group Yum Brands — would further trim the potential cost savings.

Perhaps it’s just that Niccol could use some more motivation. After all, the generous $100mn-plus package he received in 2024, linked to the company’s share price, has mostly failed to pay out. Worse, having started his role in sunny California, he now spends significant time in rainy Seattle. Starbucks should want to keep Niccol engaged, but buying Chipotle is too high a price.
john.foley@ft.com

Chipotle Jumps on Report Starbucks Has Explored Takeover 

Summary by Bloomberg AI
▪Chipotle Mexican Grill Inc. shares jumped after the Financial Times reported that Starbucks Corp. has worked with advisers on a takeover proposal for the burrito chain.
▪The status of the takeover plans couldn’t be immediately learned and a mega deal of this size might never get off the ground, according to people familiar with the matter.

By Redd Brown
10/08/2026 09:51:46 [BN]

(Bloomberg) -- Chipotle Mexican Grill Inc. shares jumped +8% after the Financial Times reported that Starbucks Corp. has worked with advisers in recent months on a takeover proposal for the burrito chain.

The status of the takeover plans couldn’t be immediately learned and a mega deal of this size might never get off the ground, the Times said, citing people familiar with the matter. Brian Niccol, Starbucks’ chief executive officer since 2024, previously spent six years as the top executive at Chipotle, where he spearheaded a period of rapid growth.

Starbucks declined to comment on the FT report, and a spokesperson for Chipotle couldn’t be reached for comment.

Chipotle shares surged as much as 8.6% in New York trading on Thursday. The stock has fallen about 20% over the past year. Starbucks declined as much as 6.7%, the most intraday in more than a year, before paring its drop.

Starbucks is in the midst of a broad turnaround strategy that touches on everything from its store design to how fast its beverages are made to its food lineup. Niccol has complained that its food counters don’t look bountiful enough and said he doesn’t like the cardboard signage that displays photos of its food menu. 

Chipotle Mexican Grill Inc. shares jumped after the Financial Times reported that Starbucks Corp. has reportedly worked with advisers in recent months on a takeover proposal for Chipotle. Michael Halen of Bloomberg Intelligence has more.

Analysts expressed skepticism about a potential deal given the vast differences between the two businesses. Additionally, Chipotle’s market cap is about $41 billion, and a potential acquisition would rank among the largest ever in the restaurant sector, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

“Initially, it doesn’t seem like there’s that many synergies for something like this to happen,” Melius Research analyst Jacob Aiken-Phillips said in an interview. “Obviously, Brian Niccol has intimate knowledge of Chipotle’s operations and Chipotle has pulled back a ton, but I’d have to hear a lot more about what the potential plan would be to see if there’s actually anything to be gained.”

Aiken-Phillips added that access to Chipotle’s supply chain and Starbucks’ recent efforts to improve its food offerings could provide some justification for the potential overture.

“Chipotle has purchasing scale of all these good, fresh ingredients and relationships across the country, so certainly that could help, but it’s not like Starbucks has a grill,” he said.

With news that oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz are approaching pre-war levels, we decided to dig into the data for a fuller picture. We looked at total exports of oil and petroleum products from Persian Gulf countries (including Oman). That means all bypass routes and ports outside the strait and counting only those shipments that deliver to global markets, including ship-to-ship transfers. At the end of the day, that is what matters for the global economy. Here's what we found:

1. As of September 30, oil exports (on a seven day average basis) are indeed approaching pre-war levels -- 23.3 million barrels per day compared to the 2025 average of about 24.6 million barrels per day. 

2. That headline number masks a big shift, however. Crude exports are now ABOVE the 2025 average, while refined product exports continue to lag -- down 30% as of September 30 compared to 2025. This isn't entirely surprising. The economics of the current shuttling system work better for 2-million-barrel crude tankers than smaller product tankers; the former can spread the (reported) $40 million fees across more barrels. Also, the major bypass pipelines through Saudi and UAE are built for crude. 

3. Based on our analysis, the world has lost more than 2.2 billion barrels of Persian Gulf crude and product exports since the war began -- about a quarter of the region’s 2025 annual exports. 

The recovery is real. But with Iranian attacks on vessels intensifying again, it may also be fragile.

During the inflationary pressures of 2022, we created our "MORTGAS" consumer misery index that is simply a sum of the price of gas ($/gallon) and the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate.

Our MORTGAS index hit a record low in the early 2020s when mortgage rates got below 3% and prices at the pump briefly got below $2/gallon.  Those days are long gone.

Gas prices first spiked in early 2022 when Russia invaded Ukraine, then they trended lower for the next few years until they spiked again this year with the US invasion of Iran.

Mortgage rates went from 3% up to 7% during the Fed's massive tightening cycle to address runaway inflation in 2022.  They too had been trending lower over the past few years, but they've moved higher again this year since the Iran War began.

Combined, our MORTGAS index is actually at a new record high right now, eclipsing the peak seen back in October 2023.  Consumers are feeling the pain as we head into midterm elections less than a month away.

posts.text:
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq are trading less than 1% from their all-time highs. Although the major indexes largely avoided the typical August–September correction, significant weakness occurred beneath the surface. Many individual stocks corrected below key moving averages, breadth deteriorated, and equal-weighted indexes weakened while mega-cap strength supported the capitalization-weighted indexes. In effect, the market experienced a stealth correction, stock by stock.

Evidence of that stealth correction can be seen clearly in market breadth. Despite the major indexes trading at or near all-time highs, the percentage of stocks trading above their 50- and 200-day moving averages has fallen to historically low levels. In fact, we have seen some of the lowest participation above these key moving averages ever recorded with the major indexes at or near all-time highs. That is an unusually large divergence between what the headline indexes are showing and what is actually happening beneath the surface.

That could provide an interesting setup entering a historically favorable Q4, particularly during a midterm election year. If breadth improves and previously corrected stocks stabilize and regain their key moving averages, participation could broaden and strengthen the advance. Even without significant broadening, historical seasonality still favors the major indexes moving higher into year-end.

Small-cap stocks, emerging markets, and many cyclical areas have lagged, leaving market gains increasingly concentrated among a handful of large-cap leaders. The resilience of AI-related themes, despite broader market weakness, continues to support the case for technology-oriented exposure.

The primary complication remains interest rates and inflation. Nominal GDP growth remains strong, but historically the 10-year Treasury yield has averaged roughly 200–250 basis points above the GDP deflator; recently, that spread has been closer to 100 basis points. Either inflation needs to moderate and validate current yields, or Treasury yields may still have further to rise. A 10-year yield peaking near 5.25%, particularly alongside moderating inflation, would be constructive for equities. A decisive move above that level with inflation remaining elevated could create a significant headwind.

Investors are also becoming increasingly discriminating about credit risk, with signs of widening spreads between lower-quality high-yield debt and investment-grade bonds. While the move is not yet indicative of a full-blown credit stress event, it represents another potential warning developing beneath the surface. When investors begin demanding greater compensation for owning lower-quality debt while equities remain near record highs, it can signal that risk perceptions are changing before those concerns become evident in the major stock indexes.

For now, the trend remains positive, but selectivity is important. Focus on high-quality stocks emerging from sound bases with strong or improving relative strength and favorable price-volume characteristics. Most important, cut losses on all stock that fail, and only get aggressive on the heels of traction. NO FORCED TRADES. NO BIG LOSSES.

The key question for Q4 is whether improving breadth and favorable seasonality can reinforce the uptrend—or whether persistent inflation, rising yields, and renewed distribution undermine it.

After yesterday's aggressive tech selloff, triggered by concerns surrounding OpenAI's revenue miss, stocks are bouncing back in today's premarket. 

But this is not an environment to aggressively chase strength. The major indices are holding up relatively well, while many individual momentum stocks continue to suffer significant technical damage.

*

The recent pullback in $SPY looks relatively normal after an extended advance toward $781. 

#SPY tested its 8-day moving average, shook out aggressive momentum traders, and held important support around $770. 

Now trading near $776.72 in the premarket, it faces immediate resistance at yesterday's $777 high and the $779 area. 

I doubt SPY can push decisively above that zone today. It could offer a tactical opportunity to reestablish some short exposure.

*

Similar story in $QQQ. After a strong multi-day rally that left the Nasdaq extended above its 8-day moving average, profit-taking was overdue. 

Yesterday's selloff brought #QQQ back toward that average, filled the previously identified gap near $743, and tested an important neckline. 

The action was sloppy, but the broader technical structure hasn't necessarily broken down. Still, a rebound doesn't automatically mean momentum has returned.

*

$SPCX  continues to be one of the few names that is still demonstrates relatively constructive momentum. 

After three consecutive down days into support, #SPCX is surging roughly $6 toward $166 in the premarket despite approximately 7% of its float becoming available for sale. 

I missed the entry near yesterday's close but I am not chasing the gap higher. 

Let the opening selling pressure play out, watch whether SPCX holds up during the first 30 minutes, and assess whether buyers can reclaim the previous topping-tail candle. 

Strong relative performance is encouraging, but entry price matters.

*

There is a growing divergence among semiconductors and memory-related stocks.

$MU is technically fine, but far from special. The stock continues to frustrate breakout traders with sideways action, failed momentum attempts, and limited follow-through. 

I would maintain disciplined positions around established support rather than repeatedly chasing rallies. A premarket bounce doesn't change the need for confirmation.

$SNDK technical picture is deteriorating. #SNDK is rolling below important moving averages, including the 50-day. I see little reason to chase until the stock stabilizes.

$WDC  is even weaker, with shares slipping below the 200-day moving average. This is not the kind of technical setup I would want to trade aggressively.

*

So, yesterday's selloff may have created a short-term rebound opportunity, but it hasn't repaired the damage beneath the surface. 

$SPY and $QQQ remain relatively resilient, yet failed breakouts, weak momentum, and deteriorating individual charts demand your caution.

Don't confuse a bounce with a sustainable breakout. Stay selective, respect resistance, avoid chasing opening gaps, and wait for the market to prove that buyers are genuinely back in control.

$USO is also worth watching.

I've reduced risk, taken profits, and am keeping positions relatively small. Rather than chasing strength, I am watching how leading stocks behave at support.
